The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning.
Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.
We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.




Synthesizing decks and their reasoning


There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. 
Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:
"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."
The coder reasons about geometry:
"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."
The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.
The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.
What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.




Steering a deck in plain English


Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:
## Rollout plan
- March: pilot with two teams
- May: security review complete
- July: rollout to all of engineering
- September: company-wide launch
- November: first adoption review
[[make this a timeline]]

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.
The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Category
Example directive



Layout
[[make this a timeline]]


Tone
[[be candid, no spin]]


Audience
[[this is for the board]]


Order
[[lead with the ask]]


Leaving out
[[no pricing]]


Emphasis
[[highlight the headline number]]





Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.




Building a check-and-repair harness


Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.
First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.
The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).
To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.




Evaluation


We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.
Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.
PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.




What's next


The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.
We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.




What we learned


Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:
Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone.
Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output.
Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output.
Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship.

summaries.en: Palette teaches a small open-weight model to build custom slide decks in a user's design language by training it on synthetic data and using a human-like designer-coder approach. The model, fine-tuned on the IBM Design Language, ranks first on two domains in PresentBench. This method ensures deck ownership and avoids AI defaults while maintaining quality.

items.title: CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency
items.content:
Update on GitHub

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

  • Does the instruction read like a realistic instruction and not an evaluation setting?
  • Can every graded behaviour be inferred from the instruction?
  • Does the verifier check for correct behaviour and not for specific structure of one fix?
  • Does the starter code fail and the reference fix pass?
  • Does the original functionality still work with the new fix?
  • Do the verifiers fail memorized solutions like the known upstream patch?

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Run it from the Hub

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

harbor run --repo "https://huggingface.co/datasets/collinear-ai/cwe-bench" -d cwe-bench@2.0 -k 4 \
  --agent <agent> --model <model> --env docker \
  --allow-agent-host <model API host>

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

hf auth login --token $HF_TOKEN --add-to-git-credential

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

items.title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
items.content:
Update on GitHub

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Why bugs reach main

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

Introducing Model Integration Contracts

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

  • a fixture: the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned
  • a usage path: a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step
  • baselines: the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

inputs = tokenizer("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=4, do_sample=False)
new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
print(tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True))

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

The UMT5 regression

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

How models are shrunk

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

The recipe now has four steps:

  1. Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name.
  2. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test.
  3. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds.
  4. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Building MICs with agents

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git"
hf auth login
tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to ''

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Random vs Overfit

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

  • Start with random weights and a fixed seed.
  • Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris".

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

Open questions

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

  • How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays?
  • How often does it send us chasing false alarms?
  • How much work do baseline reviews take?

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-*
checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and
checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5
bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.
Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a
chance to catch bugs before they reach main.




Introducing Model Integration Contracts


transformers-mic is a proposed
standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has
three parts:
a fixture: the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned
a usage path: a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the
model, such as generating text or running a training step
baselines: the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a
human
The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the
baselines.
A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint:
compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected
results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.
For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital
of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading
the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:
inputs = tokenizer("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=4, do_sample=False)
new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
print(tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True))

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies
that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full
usage.md.
A fleet dataset
on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions
used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it
used, so we can reproduce it later.
On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.




The UMT5 regression


We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small
UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026
until its fix on September 28.
Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training
loss by about 0.20.
One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path.
Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only
helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.
We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check
failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step
took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.
The replay results
and the CI demo
have the measurements and reproduction details.




How models are shrunk


The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer
layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no
use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.
The recipe now has four steps:
Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce
hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds,
including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers.
Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible.
We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in
test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we
take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name.
Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and
input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte.
Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test.
Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change
the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training
it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and
check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds.
Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable
outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each
supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses
it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR.
We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the
conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint.
The full recipe
has more detail.
The Llama 4 Scout shrink report
shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7
million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from
48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.




Building MICs with agents


Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new
model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure
the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed
expectations require human review.
To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:
pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git"
hf auth login
tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to ''

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your
machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything.
For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed
to your own account (--bill-to ''). The
CLI docs
cover the individual steps.
We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge
case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from
model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the
coverage space.




Random vs Overfit


With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in
the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.
So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green".
We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible
in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study,
the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit
fixtures caught all 24.
That gives us two ways to build the weights:
Start with random weights and a fixed seed.
Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris".
The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic
faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit
version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper
checkpoint exposed.
So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need
better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one
more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison
has the results for both.




Open questions


As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI
reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on
things we haven't measured yet:
How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays?
How often does it send us chasing false alarms?
How much work do baseline reviews take?
We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only
show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.
Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use.
When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay
it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their
coverage is accounted for.
Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a
developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on
that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.
Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the
coverage space, try
the tmic workflow,
and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

items.title: Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software
items.content:
Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

  1. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass.
  2. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

items.title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
items.content:
Update on GitHub

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Making publicly funded science more usable

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Open Science Challenges

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

  • Demonstrate scientific reuse. Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines.
  • Learn what makes reuse possible. Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

The first challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

How to Join Project ProtoStar

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

items.title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

  1. FP8
  2. NVFP4

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Table of Contents

  • "Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face"
    • Table of Contents
    • What is new with Mistral Large 4
      • Cybersecurity Capabilities
    • Architecture
      • Vision encoder
    • Benchmark Results
    • Inference Support
      • Transformers
      • vLLM
      • Llama.cpp
    • Fine-tuning with TRL
    • Inference Endpoints
    • Dell Enterprise Hub
    • Try it out

What is new with Mistral Large 4

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Cybersecurity Capabilities

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Architecture

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.


For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.
The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Vision encoder

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Benchmark Results

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

  • Artificial Analysis Cyber Index: ML4 ranks among the top five models globally on this independent evaluation of models’ ability to find and fix software vulnerabilities.
  • Vulnerability reproduction and patching: It achieves 82%, the highest reported score on this test within the index. The task requires reproducing a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patching it, testing both investigation and remediation.
  • Cybench: ML4 solves 93% of a suite of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions, demonstrating strong performance on hands-on security problems.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Inference Support

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

Transformers

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

To run the model, upgrade the transformers package

pip install --upgrade transformers

import os
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig

distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
    tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
    ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
)

model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=distributed_config,
)

# only text
text_messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Who are you?"
    }
]

# text + image
multimodal_messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "image",
                "image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg",
            },
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": "How many cats are in the image?",
            },
        ],
    },
]

for messages in [text_messages, multimodal_messages]:
    inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
        messages,
        add_generation_prompt=True,
        tokenize=True,
        return_dict=True,
        return_tensors="pt",
        reasoning_effort="medium",
    ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
    input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100)
    if int(os.environ["RANK"]) == 0:
        print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

You can run the script above by saving it in a python file script.py and then run

torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py

vLLM

vLLM supports the high-quality NVFP4 Mistral Large 4 checkpoint, which has a smaller memory footprint and requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. The model also ships with a DSpark drafter for additional speed-ups with vLLM. Launch the server like this:

vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
  --config-format mistral \
  --load-format mistral \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --decode-context-parallel-size 8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 131072 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --enforce-eager \
  --mm_processor_cache_gb 0.0

Once the server is up and running, you can run the following.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 17*23?"}],"max_tokens":512}'

Llama.cpp

Llama.cpp and Llama App already support Mistral Large 4.

You can install Llama App with the following command:

curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh

Then you can start the server as follows, indicating the quant suffix after the model ID:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF:Q2_K

Here’s the repository with the quants derived from the FP8 checkpoint, and this is the NVFP4 one, converted from the official NVFP4 repo.

Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat using the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.
You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ]
    }'

You can run image-text inference as follows.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
    -d '{
        "model": "muse-spark-open",
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": [
                    {
                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "What is in this image?"
                    },
                    {
                        "type": "image_url",
                        "image_url": {
                            "url": "data:image/png;base64,..."
                        }
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "temperature": 0
    }'

The llama.cpp team ships the following quants: IQ2_XXS, Q2_K, Q4_K_M, NVFP4, Q8_0, and BF16 for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.

Running Q2_K on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results:

  • NVFP4: 32K context size, prefill 130-590 t/s, gen speed ~10 t/s
  • IQ2_XXS: 800K context size. At short context sizes, prefill is 500 tok/s and generation runs at 30 tok/s. However, using long contexts performance drops to 129 tok/s (prefill) and 3 tok/s (generation).

Fine-tuning with TRL

We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of transformers, trl and peft.

pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft

In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for!

The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in TRL's examples.

# torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 sft.py
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size),
    dtype="auto",
)

dataset = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking", split="train")
# the assistant turns carry reasoning, so render them in reasoning mode
dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: {"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "high"}})

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(
        packing=True,
        max_length=4096,
        assistant_only_loss=True,
        learning_rate=1e-4,
        lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
        warmup_steps=10,
    ),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(
        r=16,
        lora_alpha=32,
        target_modules=r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)",
    ),
)
trainer.train()

Inference Endpoints

Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results:

  • Single request: time to first token of about 0.6 seconds for a 1K-token prompt, and a generation speed of ~65 tok/s, reaching 120–138 tok/s on chat prompts where DSpark's drafts are accepted.
  • Long prompts: 16K-token prompts, four at a time, are prefilled at about 4,300 tok/s in total, with a time to first token of 8–9 seconds.
  • Under load: about 480 tok/s of total generation across 1,000 ShareGPT conversations.

You can deploy it with the hf CLI as follows:

hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --name mistral-large-4

Once the endpoint is running, you can query its OpenAI-compatible API, using the endpoint URL and your Hugging Face token. The reasoning_effort field controls how much the model reasons before answering, and can be set to low, medium, or high (default).

curl "$(hf endpoints describe mistral-large-4 --json | jq -r .status.url)/v1/chat/completions" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token 2>/dev/null)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
        "model": "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B",
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ],
        "reasoning_effort": "medium"
    }'

The answer comes back in choices[0].message.content, and the reasoning in choices[0].message.reasoning. The endpoint also supports tool calls, structured outputs, image inputs, and streaming through the standard Chat Completions fields.

Dell Enterprise Hub

The easiest way to get up and running with your Dell AI Servers (NVIDIA H200, B200, GB200 or GB300) is by installing the dell-ai CLI:

pip install dell-ai && dell-ai login

And use it to run an optimized recipe for Mistral Large 4 on e.g., a NVIDIA B300 node.

dell-ai models deploy --model-id mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
    --engine docker \
    --platform-id xe9780-nvidia-b300 \
    --gpus 4

You can find more about this release in the Dell Enterprise Hub (DEH).

Try it out

Grab the weights from the Mistral Large 4 collection, run them locally with the GGUFs, or deploy them with Inference Endpoints. We can't wait to see what you build with Le Chonk. Share your fine-tunes, quants and other artefacts on the Hub!

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
    -d '{
        "model": "muse-spark-open",
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": [
                    {
                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "What is in this image?"
                    },
                    {
                        "type": "image_url",
                        "image_url": {
                            "url": "data:image/png;base64,..."
                        }
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "temperature": 0
    }'

The llama.cpp team ships the following quants: IQ2_XXS, Q2_K, Q4_K_M, NVFP4, Q8_0, and BF16 for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.
Running Q2_K on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results:
NVFP4: 32K context size, prefill 130-590 t/s, gen speed ~10 t/s  
IQ2_XXS: 800K context size. At short context sizes, prefill is 500 tok/s and generation runs at 30 tok/s. However, using long contexts performance drops to 129 tok/s (prefill) and 3 tok/s (generation).




Fine-tuning with TRL


We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of transformers, trl and peft.
pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft

In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for!
The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in TRL's examples.
# torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 sft.py
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size),
    dtype="auto",
)

dataset = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking", split="train")
# the assistant turns carry reasoning, so render them in reasoning mode
dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: {"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "high"}})

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(
        packing=True,
        max_length=4096,
        assistant_only_loss=True,
        learning_rate=1e-4,
        lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
        warmup_steps=10,
    ),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(
        r=16,
        lora_alpha=32,
        target_modules=r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)",
    ),
)
trainer.train()





Inference Endpoints


Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results:
Single request: time to first token of about 0.6 seconds for a 1K-token prompt, and a generation speed of ~65 tok/s, reaching 120–138 tok/s on chat prompts where DSpark's drafts are accepted.  
Long prompts: 16K-token prompts, four at a time, are prefilled at about 4,300 tok/s in total, with a time to first token of 8–9 seconds.  
Under load: about 480 tok/s of total generation across 1,000 ShareGPT conversations.
You can deploy it with the hf CLI as follows:
hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --name mistral-large-4

Once the endpoint is running, you can query its OpenAI-compatible API, using the endpoint URL and your Hugging Face token. The reasoning_effort field controls how much the model reasons before answering, and can be set to low, medium, or high (default).
curl "$(hf endpoints describe mistral-large-4 --json | jq -r .status.url)/v1/chat/completions" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token 2>/dev/null)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
        "model": "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B",
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ],
        "reasoning_effort": "medium"
    }'

The answer comes back in choices[0].message.content, and the reasoning in choices[0].message.reasoning. The endpoint also supports tool calls, structured outputs, image inputs, and streaming through the standard Chat Completions fields.




Dell Enterprise Hub


The easiest way to get up and running with your Dell AI Servers (NVIDIA H200, B200, GB200 or GB300) is by installing the dell-ai CLI:
pip install dell-ai && dell-ai login

And use it to run an optimized recipe for Mistral Large 4 on e.g., a NVIDIA B300 node.
dell-ai models deploy --model-id mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
    --engine docker \
    --platform-id xe9780-nvidia-b300 \
    --gpus 4

You can find more about this release in the Dell Enterprise Hub (DEH).




Try it out


Grab the weights from the Mistral Large 4 collection, run them locally with the GGUFs, or deploy them with Inference Endpoints. We can't wait to see what you build with Le Chonk. Share your fine-tunes, quants and other artefacts on the Hub!
