items.title: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:

  • AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when.
  • AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

AnySpeechRecognizer

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

- import Speech
+ import AnySpeechRecognizer

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
    model: ParakeetSpeechModel(variant: .v3),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [.volatileResults],
    attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
)

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Meet the models

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
    model: QwenSpeechModel(variant: .large, language: Locale.Language(identifier: "yue")),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [],
    attributeOptions: []
)

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

Core ML models on the Hub

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Model Core ML conversion Original checkpoint License
Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 mattt/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-coreml nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 CC BY 4.0
Parakeet Ultra mattt/parakeet-ultra-coreml moondream/parakeet-ultra CC BY 4.0
Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B mattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coreml nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b NVIDIA Open Model License
Qwen3-ASR 0.6B mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf Apache 2.0
Qwen3-ASR 1.7B mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf Apache 2.0
Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2 CC BY 4.0
Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 NVIDIA Open Model License

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Speaker diarization

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer(model: SortformerDiarizationModel())
if let request = try await AssetInventory.assetInstallationRequest(
    supporting: [transcriber, diarizer]
) {
    try await request.downloadAndInstall()
}
let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(modules: [transcriber, diarizer])

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

How well does it work?

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Transcriber test-clean test-other
Parakeet v3, file 1.55% 2.78%
Parakeet v3, live 4.73% 4.29%
Parakeet Ultra, file 1.66% 2.55%
Parakeet Ultra, live 2.65% 3.28%
Parakeet Unified, file 1.43% 2.19%
Parakeet Unified, live 1.45% 2.42%
Apple's transcriber, file 2.12% 3.97%

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

import AnyDecisionModel

enum Department: String, Choosable {
    case billing, technical, sales
}

let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund."

let model = MLXDecisionModel(modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit")
let session = DecisionSession(model: model, state: .text(ticket))

let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?")
let team = try await session.choice("Which team?", from: Department.self)
let anger = try await session.score(
    "How frustrated?",
    levels: ["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"]
)

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice<Department> containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Try it out: Emoji Magnet

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true?

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Decision heads and Clef

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

let model = MLXHeadDecisionModel(
    modelID: "mlx-community/clef-flash-4bit",
    head: .jointSchema
)

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Calibrating and checking probabilities

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

Backends

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:

  • MLX runs a small language model on Apple silicon with mlx-swift-lm and downloads it from the Hub.
  • MLX decision heads run a model with its own trained decision head, such as Clef.
  • Core AI does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27.
  • llama.cpp reads decisions from a local GGUF model through llama.swift.
  • Jev calls TypeSafe's Jev through the System One API, or any server that implements it, such as Kev.
  • Ollama calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server or in Ollama's cloud. It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Get started

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:

dependencies: [
    .package(url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer", from: "0.1.0"),
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel",
        from: "0.6.0",
        traits: ["MLX"]
    ),
]

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Links

  • AnySpeechRecognizer on GitHub
  • AnyDecisionModel on GitHub
  • AnyDecisionModel-Examples on GitHub
  • AnyLanguageModel on GitHub
  • swift-huggingface on GitHub

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds,
without volatile results, word timing, or confidence.
It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet,
so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.
To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration
and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session.
The README includes a small provider
that reports placeholder text to help you get started.




Core ML models on the Hub


To run these models in apps,
we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint
and a checksum for every file,
and the package pins it to a fixed revision.
The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input,
which cuts live analysis time by about a third
at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate.
The repository also has the conversion workflows,
most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts,
and checks each conversion against the original model.
Downloads happen only when your app asks for them:
about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder,
0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer.
Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache,
so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.




Speaker diarization


When you transcribe a conversation,
you often want to know who said what.
That's speaker diarization,
and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it,
so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one.
SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's
Streaming Sortformer
on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber,
on the same timeline:
let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer(model: SortformerDiarizationModel())
if let request = try await AssetInventory.assetInstallationRequest(
    supporting: [transcriber, diarizer]
) {
    try await request.downloadAndInstall()
}
let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(modules: [transcriber, diarizer])

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers,
even when they talk over each other.
A SpeakerTimeline collects its results
and attributes each timed word to a speaker,
so you can print a transcript by speaker turn.
Like image support in AnyLanguageModel,
this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.
The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default.
You can also choose v2.1,
which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data
and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.




How well does it work?


We measured the package with its hear command-line tool
on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1.
Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio
in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file,
or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live,
with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model.
Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory.
Meetings are hard for everyone:
on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other,
every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.
These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets,
so measure with your own hardware and audio.
hear evaluate works on your own files,
and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool
reproduces these measurements.
So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.
Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.




AnyDecisionModel


AnyDecisionModel is a different story.
There's no Apple framework to map onto,
and decision models aren't new, exactly.
It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France;
otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.
What's new is the name, a lot of hype,
and a crop of models trained to make decisions.
We think that's where things are going,
so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.
Apps often ask language models to make decisions.
Is this message urgent?
Which team should handle this ticket?
How frustrated is this customer?
The usual approach is to prompt a language model
and parse the text that it generates.
That gives you one answer,
but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.
Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:
import AnyDecisionModel

enum Department: String, Choosable {
    case billing, technical, sales
}

let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund."

let model = MLXDecisionModel(modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit")
let session = DecisionSession(model: model, state: .text(ticket))

let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?")
let team = try await session.choice("Which team?", from: Department.self)
let anger = try await session.score(
    "How frustrated?",
    levels: ["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"]
)

urgent is a Double.
team is a Choice<Department> containing the selected case,
a probability for each option, and a confidence value.
anger is a Score containing the expected level,
a probability for each level, and a confidence value.
Because Department conforms to Choosable,
team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.
If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel,
the model-and-session pattern will look familiar.
A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON,
and every question is about that state.
Questions are independent:
an answer never becomes input to a later question.
To ask several questions at once,
pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.
For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt
with a one-token label for each allowed answer,
then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.




Try it out: Emoji Magnet



Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji.
Type a phrase, such as "things you wear",
and the emoji that match rise out of the pile.
Refine it to "things you wear in winter",
and the emoji that no longer match fall back.
The app has no built-in keyword rules;
the model decides everything at inference time.
When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji,
for example:
Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true?

The session's state holds the phrase.
The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend,
which answers all 343 questions in one request,
so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase.
Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend.
That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once,
then answers 16 questions per forward pass.
On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads.
A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds,
and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.
Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.




Decision heads and Clef


Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models,
but those models weren't trained to make decisions.
Cloudflare's Clef models
are an example of a newer approach:
a model with a trained decision head
that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions,
returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions
in one forward pass.
Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.
AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:
let model = MLXHeadDecisionModel(
    modelID: "mlx-community/clef-flash-4bit",
    head: .jointSchema
)

You use the same sessions and questions,
but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head
instead of from next-token probabilities.
The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download,
and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory.
Clef can read images and video,
but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.




Calibrating and checking probabilities


Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident.
The local backends accept a Calibration,
which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers.
Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.
Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list.
On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends,
turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question
once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities.
That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.
Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value
based on the entropy of its probabilities.
It measures how concentrated the probabilities are,
not whether the answer is right,
so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold.
The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability
the model assigned to the allowed answers.
A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.




Backends


AnyDecisionModel has six backends:
MLX runs a small language model on Apple silicon
with mlx-swift-lm
and downloads it from the Hub.
MLX decision heads run a model with its own trained decision head,
such as Clef.
Core AI does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27.
llama.cpp reads decisions from a local GGUF model
through llama.swift.
Jev calls TypeSafe's Jev through the System One API,
or any server that implements it, such as Kev.
Ollama calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server
or in Ollama's cloud.
It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models.
The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9,
so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels.
Decision heads have no such limit.
Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits.
Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies.
You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends,
which also build on Linux.
Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.




Get started


Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later.
The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon.
AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later
and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.
Add the packages to your Package.swift:
dependencies: [
    .package(url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer", from: "0.1.0"),
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel",
        from: "0.6.0",
        traits: ["MLX"]
    ),
]

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer,
because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0
and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.
Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends.
AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear,
that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results.
Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen;
run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis
to install the needed assets.
Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't.
Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.




Links

AnyDecisionModel on GitHub
AnyDecisionModel-Examples on GitHub
AnyLanguageModel on GitHub

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra,
to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects
documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow,
to Cloudflare for Clef,
and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel,
whose patterns both packages borrow.

AnySpeechRecognizer offers choices of speech-to-text engines like NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR, supporting speaker diarization. items.title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
items.content:
LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

  • More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.
  • Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model.
  • Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device.
  • Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment.

How we built a more expressive backbone

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

  1. Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.
  2. Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization.
  3. Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE.
  4. Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled.

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

One backbone for six models

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

Model Input Output Built on
LFM3-1.7B Text Text LFM3-1.7B-Base
LFM3-VL-2B Text, images, video Text LFM3 backbone + vision encoder
LFM3-Audio-2B Text, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec
LFM3-Omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder
d1-2B Text, images, video Calibrated answers LFM3-VL-2B
d1-omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Calibrated answers LFM3-Omni-2B

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

  • Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length.
  • Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.

How to use the LFM3 models

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

LFM3-1.7B

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

pip install -U transformers

Then load and run the model:

from transformers import pipeline

generator = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is C. elegans?"}]
output = generator(
    messages,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.1,
    max_new_tokens=2048,
)
print(output[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

LFM3-VL-2B

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow

Then load and run the model:

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B"

model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True)
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "url": "https://placecats.com/300/200"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image."},
        ],
    }
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)

with torch.inference_mode():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        do_sample=True,
        temperature=0.1,
        top_k=50,
        repetition_penalty=1.1,
        max_new_tokens=16384,  # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long
    )

generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
print(processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

LFM3-Audio-2B

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

import torch
import soundfile as sf

from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code=True
).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device).eval()

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

conversation = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "Respond with interleaved text and audio."},
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio", "audio": "question.wav"}]},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "<|mixed_start|>"},
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    continue_final_message=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        max_new_tokens=1024,
        audio_temperature=1.0,
        audio_top_k=128,
        audio_repetition_penalty=1.1,
        audio_repetition_window=4096,
        return_dict_in_generate=True,
    )

    text = processor.decode(
        outputs.sequences[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:],
        skip_special_tokens=True,
    )
    waveform = codec.decode(
        outputs.audio_codes[:1, :, :outputs.audio_lengths[0]]
    ).audio_values[0]  # 24 kHz
print(text)
sf.write("reply.wav", waveform.float().cpu().numpy(), 24_000)

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

LFM3-Omni-2B

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile

import torch
import soundfile as sf

from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code=True
).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device).eval()

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

conversation = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text.",
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "photo.jpg"},
            {"type": "audio", "audio": "question.wav"},
        ],
    },
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.
LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:
More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.  
Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model.  
Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device.  
Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment.




How we built a more expressive backbone


LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:
Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.  
Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization.  
Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE.  
Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled.
The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.




One backbone for six models


Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:
Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length.  
Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.




How to use the LFM3 models


Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.




LFM3-1.7B


Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps.     trust_remote_code=True,
)

    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.1,
    max_new_tokens=2048,
)

items.title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
items.content:
Update on GitHub

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

Look up a model

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Run it yourself

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

python3 run.py

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache

What "runs" means

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

The results are a dataset

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet("hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data")
df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"][["neuronx_cc", "library", "library_version", "neuron_cores", "result"]]

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.
